title: Welcome to Harborne Museum
context: A recorded welcome talk introduces visitors to a local history museum and explains how to find their way around.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Welcome to Harborne Museum, and thank you for picking up an audio guide. Before you start exploring, let me quickly explain how the museum is organised, so you don't miss anything.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: It should only take an hour or so to see everything properly, though of course you're welcome to take as long as you like.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The museum has three floors. The ground floor covers the town's early history, from its beginnings as a small fishing village right up to the arrival of the railway. The first floor, upstairs, is dedicated to the industrial period, when the town's population grew rapidly because of the new textile mills. And the second floor, right at the top, is our temporary exhibition space, which changes every few months.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The ground floor in particular has grown quite a lot over the years, as local families keep donating items that turn out to have been sitting in an attic for generations, forgotten about until someone finally cleared the house out.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: I should mention that the current temporary exhibition was originally going to be about local shipbuilding, but that's been postponed until next year. Instead, the second floor currently holds an exhibition on wartime life in the town, which runs until the end of this year.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: It's proved to be one of our most popular exhibitions yet, with photographs and letters kindly lent by families who still live locally.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: As you move around, look out for the small blue numbers on the wall beside certain objects. These correspond to numbered stops on this audio guide — just press the matching number on your handset to hear more.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: If you'd rather not carry the handset the whole time, there's also a small rack of printed guides at the entrance desk covering the same stops.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: One object not to miss is on the ground floor: a wooden fishing boat, over two hundred years old, which was actually found buried in mud near the old harbour rather than kept above ground the whole time, which is part of why it survived so well.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Conservators worked on it for several years before it went on display, and you can still see a few of the original iron fittings along the hull.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: If you get hungry, the café is on the ground floor, near the main entrance, and serves light lunches until three p.m. After that, only drinks and cakes are available, so do plan your lunch break accordingly.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The soup is made fresh on site every morning, and it's usually the first thing to sell out, so I'd get there in good time if that's what you fancy. There's also a small terrace outside for anyone who'd rather sit in the fresh air.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Toilets are located on every floor, but the accessible toilet is only on the ground floor, next to the cloakroom.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: There's also a baby-changing table in there, and a small lockers area if you'd rather not carry bags and coats round with you.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Photography is welcome throughout the museum, but please don't use flash near the textile exhibits on the first floor, as the strong light can damage the fabric over time.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Tripods aren't permitted anywhere in the building, I'm afraid, simply because the galleries get too busy for them to be practical.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The museum shop is on the ground floor as well, close to the exit, and sells books, postcards, and replicas of some of the smaller objects on display.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: A good number of the postcards are actually reproductions of photographs from our own archive, so you won't find them anywhere else in the town.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: We close at five p.m. on weekdays, but stay open later, until seven p.m., on Thursdays, to give people who work during the day a chance to visit after their working hours.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Do keep an eye on the clock towards the end of your visit, as we do need everyone to have left the galleries a little before the doors actually lock. Staff will start gently reminding people shortly beforehand, so don't be alarmed if someone taps you on the shoulder.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: That's everything you need to get started. Enjoy your visit, and remember, if you have any questions at all, our staff in green jackets are happy to help throughout the museum.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Once again, welcome to Harborne Museum, and I hope you enjoy exploring everything we have to offer today.

questions.question: What does the ground floor mainly cover?
options: the industrial period of the town
the town's early history up to the railway
wartime life in the town and villages
questions.explanation: The ground floor covers "the town's early history, from its beginnings as a small fishing village right up to the arrival of the railway."

questions.question: Why should visitors avoid using flash photography on the first floor?
options: it disturbs the other visitors nearby
it can damage the textile exhibits over time
photography is banned in there completely
questions.explanation: Photography is allowed throughout, but flash near the textile exhibits is discouraged because "the strong light can damage the fabric over time."
